# Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the pancreas > Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors*

[Original Article Link](/library/hs0cuh)

---

## Summary

<u>Pancreatic</u> <u>neuroendocrine tumors</u> (PNETs) are <u>hormone</u>-secreting tumors of the <u>pancreas</u> that derive from <u>neuroendocrine cells</u>. The most important types are <u>glucagonomas</u>, <u>VIPomas</u>, <u>somatostatinomas</u>, <u>insulinomas</u> (treated in a separate article), and <u>gastrinomas</u> (treated in a separate article). With the exception of <u>insulinomas</u>, PNETs typically manifest with <u>diarrhea</u>, weight loss, and normal or elevated blood <u>glucose</u> levels; <u>insulinomas</u> do not affect bowel movements and manifest instead with weight gain and <u>hypoglycemia</u>. Diagnosis involves <u>laboratory studies</u> to identify excess <u>hormone</u> levels and imaging to detect the primary <u>tumor</u> and <u>metastases</u>. Surgical resection is the first-line treatment. <u>Octreotide</u> is the treatment of choice for inoperable tumors.




For more information, see “<u>Insulinoma</u>” and “<u>Gastrinoma</u>.”

## Glucagonoma

* Definition: a rare <u>neuroendocrine tumor</u> of the <u>pancreatic</u> <u>α-cells</u> that secretes <u>glucagon</u>. In > 50% of cases, <u>metastasis</u> is present at diagnosis.

* Clinical features

* Weight loss

* <u>Impaired glucose tolerance</u> or <u>diabetes mellitus</u> (75–95%)

* Necrolytic migratory erythema 

* A cutaneous <u>paraneoplastic syndrome</u> that is mainly associated with <u>pancreatic</u> tumors secreting <u>glucagon</u>, but also <u>hepatitis B</u>, C, and <u>bronchial carcinoma</u>

* Occurrence of multiple areas of <u>centrifugally</u> spreading <u>erythema</u>, located predominantly on the face, <u>perineum</u>, and lower extremities

* Develop into painful and pruritic crusty patches with central areas of bronze-colored induration

* Tend to resolve and reappear in a different location

* <u>Skin biopsy</u> shows <u>epidermal</u> <u>necrosis</u>

* <u>Chronic diarrhea</u>

* <u>Deep vein thrombosis</u>

* <u>Depression</u>

* Diagnostics: requires a high index of suspicion to make the diagnosis

* Laboratory findings: ↑ <u>glucagon</u> > 500 pg/mL, ↑ blood <u>glucose</u> levels, <u>normocytic</u> normochromic <u>anemia</u>

* Imaging (CT): to locate the <u>tumor</u>

* Treatment

* Glycemic control

* <u>Tumor</u> resection

* <u>Octreotide</u> (if <u>tumor</u> is inoperable)





> [!NOTE]
> “Wait for 6 Days until the GLUe (<u>glucagonoma</u>) is dry:” Decreasing weight, Diabetes, Dermatitis, Diarrhea, DVT, Depression.

## Somatostatinoma

* Definition: a rare <u>neuroendocrine tumor</u> of <u>δ-cell</u> (<u>D-cell</u>) origin that is usually located in the <u>pancreas</u> or <u>gastrointestinal tract</u> and secretes <u>somatostatin</u>.
* ↑ <u>Somatostatin</u> → ↓ secretion of the following <u>hormones</u>: 

* <u>Secretin</u>

* <u>Cholecystokinin</u>

* <u>Glucagon</u>

* <u>Insulin</u>

* <u>Gastrin</u>

* <u>Gastric inhibitory peptide</u>

* Clinical features

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>

* Weight loss

* Classic triad

* <u>Glucose intolerance</u>/<u>diabetes</u>

* <u>Cholelithiasis</u>

* <u>Steatorrhea</u>

* <u>Achlorhydria</u>

* Diagnostics

* Laboratory findings: ↑ <u>somatostatin</u>, ↑ blood <u>glucose</u> levels

* Imaging: locate the <u>tumor</u>

* Treatment

* <u>Tumor</u> resection: curative if no <u>metastases</u> are present

* <u>Octreotide</u> (if <u>tumor</u> is inoperable)

* <u>Chemotherapy</u>





Reference:[[4]](/library/v7bAnE)

## VIPoma

* Definition: : a <u>neuroendocrine tumor</u> that secretes <u>VIP</u> (<u>vasoactive intestinal polypeptide</u>)

* Etiology: associated with <u>MEN1</u> syndrome (5% of cases)

* Pathophysiology

* Excess <u>VIP</u> → ↑ relaxation of gastric and intestinal <u>smooth muscles</u> and <u>cAMP</u> activity (similar to <u>cholera toxin</u>) → <u>secretory diarrhea</u> and inhibition of <u>gastric acid</u> production

* <u>VIP</u> also stimulates <u>vasodilation</u>, bone resorption, and <u>glycogenolysis</u>

* <u>Tumor</u> location: The primary <u>tumor</u> is most frequently found in the <u>pancreas</u>.

* Clinical features

* WDHA syndrome (<u>watery diarrhea</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>, <u>achlorhydria</u>): tea-colored <u>watery diarrhea</u> (> 700 mL/day) → <u>dehydration</u>

* Weight loss

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Achlorhydria</u> → ↓ <u>iron</u> and B<sub>12</sub> absorption → <u>anemia</u>

* Diagnostics

* ↑ Serum <u>VIP</u> concentration (> 75 pg/mL)

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* <u>Hypercalcemia</u>  [[5]](/library/TQX6vB)

* <u>Hyperglycemia</u>

* Gastric <u>achlorhydria</u> or hypochlorhydria

* <u>CT scan</u> to localize the primary <u>tumor</u>

* Treatment

* <u>Tumor</u> resection

* <u>Octreotide</u> (inhibits <u>VIP</u> secretion)
